01.actor: A man who came before Rav Nachman
01.event: A man who had never been married told Rav Nachman he had found an unobstructed orifice on his wedding night.
01.turn: Rav Nachman doubted how he could know, since an unmarried man would have to have had experience with prostitutes.
01.outcome: Rav Nachman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
01.summary: A man who had never been married came to Rav Nachman and claimed he had found his bride's passage open, as though she were not a virgin. Rav Nachman saw that the man could only know this from experience with prostitutes. He ordered the man flogged with palm branches.

02.actor: The Sages who sent a question, and Rav
02.event: The Sages, with Mar Ukva nearby, reversed the names of the opinions of Shmuel and Karna and sent the question to Rav.
02.turn: Rav swore that she needs both a bill of divorce and refusal, and that Shmuel could not have said otherwise.
02.outcome: Rav's oath settled the ruling as Shmuel's.
02.summary: The Sages were puzzled by Shmuel's ruling that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both divorce and refusal. Mar Ukva's court was in a nearby town, but they instead sent the question to Rav with the opinions' names swapped. Rav swore that she needs both, and that Shmuel would never have said otherwise.
02.missing: It is not clear why the names were reversed, and it is not shown that the Sages ever went to Mar Ukva.

03.event: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled in accordance with the Rabbis in a case of the court's sale, or wished to.
03.turn: Perata, grandson of Perata the Great, asked what advantage the court's power would then have.
03.outcome: Rabbi reversed his ruling (Rav Dimi's version) or did not carry it out (Rav Safra's version).
03.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once ruled as the Rabbis do. Perata challenged him: if so, what advantage would the court's power have? Rabbi reversed himself. In Rav Safra's telling, Rabbi only wished to rule that way and dropped the plan when Perata objected.
03.missing: The details of the case itself are not stated.

05.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee
05.event: They bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori.
05.outcome: The Gemara asks what was remarkable about it and answers that it was costly poultry, or that an animal was slaughtered daily.
05.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a litra of meat each day for a poor man of good family from Tzippori. The text then debates what made this noteworthy, such as expensive poultry or a daily animal lost in a small village. It is a report of a practice with no turn.
05.missing: No turning point or ending is given.

06.actor: A man who deposited pearls, and Rabbi Ami
06.event: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without saying what they were.
06.turn: The claimant and the family came before Rabbi Ami in a dispute over ownership.
06.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled for the depositor, because Meyasha was not wealthy and the man gave a distinguishing mark.
06.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at the house of Rabbi Meyasha, who then died without saying anything about them. The parties came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled that they belonged to the depositor, since Meyasha was not rich and the man described the pearls accurately.

07.event: The Sages asked Rabbi Elai where Rabbi Abbahu was hiding.
07.turn: Rabbi Elai answered in a cryptic pun that he had gone to consult the Nasi and then south.
07.outcome: The riddle is explained, but nothing further happens.
07.summary: The Sages asked Rabbi Elai where Rabbi Abbahu was, and he answered with a pun that Abbahu had consulted the Nasi and gone south to the scholars there. It is a witty exchange mirroring an earlier one, with no real event or turn.
07.missing: There is no real narrative arc.

08.actor: A man who made a conditional bill of divorce
08.event: A man told his agents that his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, then arrived on the last day.
08.turn: The ferry on the other side kept him from crossing, so he shouted that he had come.
08.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this was not a return, so the condition was met and the divorce took effect.
08.summary: A man told his agents that if he did not return within thirty days, his writ would be a bill of divorce. He reached the river on the thirtieth day but the ferry was on the far side, and he shouted that he had come. Shmuel said it did not count as a return.

09.actor: Rabbi Nechemya and a man seeking charity
09.event: A man seeking help said he normally dined on fatty meat and aged wine, and Rabbi Nechemya invited him to eat lentils with him.
09.turn: He ate the lentils and died, being unused to such food.
09.outcome: Rabbi Nechemya said woe to the one he killed, which the Gemara explains as blaming the man for pampering himself.
09.summary: A man came to Rabbi Nechemya asking for charity and said he usually ate fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nechemya invited him to share lentils, and he ate them and died. The Gemara explains Nechemya's remark as meaning the man should not have pampered himself so much.

10.event: At his son's wedding, Rava served drinks to the sages.
10.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood for him, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas did not.
10.outcome: Rava became angry and asked whether the others were sages and those who stood were not.
10.summary: At his son's wedding feast Rava poured drinks for his guests. Two rabbis stood up for him, but two others stayed seated. Rava lost his temper and asked whether the first pair were sages and the second pair were not.

11.event: In a year of divine anger and famine, the Sages asked Rav Yosef to pray for mercy.
11.turn: He refused, pointing out that Elisha, who supported 2,200 scholars, did not pray in a time of famine.
11.summary: During years of famine in Rav Yosef's time, the Sages asked him to pray for mercy. He answered that Elisha, who supported 2,200 scholars, did not pray in a time of anger, so he would not either.

12.event: A woman rebelled against her husband, saying she was disgusted with him, and Mar Zutra compelled her to stay.
12.turn: Rabbi Chanina of Sura was born from the couple.
12.outcome: The Gemara dismisses it as a precedent, because that outcome came from heavenly assistance.
12.summary: A woman rebelled against her husband and said she was disgusted with him. Mar Zutra compelled her to remain with him, and from them came Rabbi Chanina of Sura. The Gemara says this is no precedent, since it was heavenly assistance.

13.actor: An unnamed man and Rav Kahana
13.event: A man let witnesses trace their names in a document other than a bill of divorce.
13.summary: A man let witnesses trace their names in an ordinary document, not a bill of divorce. Rav Kahana had him flogged. The text gives no detail beyond this single act and punishment.
13.missing: It does not say who the man was or what happened beyond the punishment.

15.event: Rabbi Yochanan's relatives, who had to pay for their father's widow's daily medical care, asked him what to do.
15.turn: He told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor so it would count as a fixed-cost treatment.
15.outcome: Later he regretted it, saying they had made themselves like legal advisors.
15.summary: Rabbi Yochanan's relatives were burdened by the daily medical costs of their father's widow and came to him. He advised them to fix a lump sum with the doctor, so the cost would come out of her marriage contract. He later regretted this, saying they had made themselves like legal advisors.

16.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya
16.event: She came before Rav Yosef asking for sustenance, wine, and silk garments.
16.turn: When he asked why she needed silk, she said it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends.
16.outcome: The text does not say whether he granted the silk.
16.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and asked for sustenance and wine, and he granted both. She then asked for silk garments. When he asked why, she said they were for him, his friends and his friends' friends, so she would not be ashamed before them.
16.missing: It is not stated whether the silk was granted.

17.actor: The son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his wife
17.event: After marrying, he spent twelve years studying in the academy, and returned to find his wife infertile.
17.turn: Rabbi said that divorce or a second wife would bring shame, so the husband prayed for her.
17.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son married and then went off to study for twelve years. On his return his wife had become infertile. Neither divorce nor a second wife seemed acceptable, so he prayed for her and she was cured.

18.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract
18.event: He sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract and told the buyer he would not reimburse him if she objected.
18.turn: His mother died without objecting, but he himself came and contested the sale.
18.outcome: Rava rejected Rami bar Chama's idea that he stands in his mother's place, saying he guaranteed against his own objections.
18.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract and said he would not repay the buyer if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he himself challenged the sale. Rava said he had taken responsibility against his own objection even if not hers.

20.event: While Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry, a man gave him a hand to help him.
20.turn: The man said he had a case to bring before Shmuel.
20.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself from judging the case.
20.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry when a man offered him a helping hand. Shmuel asked what the man wanted, and the man said he had a case. Shmuel said he was disqualified from judging it because of the favor.
